rows.label: Concept
rows.text: Inverse circular functions exist only because the trig functions are **restricted to principal branches**: sin⁻¹ on [−1,1] → **[−π/2, π/2]**, cos⁻¹ on [−1,1] → **[0, π]**, tan⁻¹ on ℝ → **(−π/2, π/2)**. Inside the branch, f⁻¹(f(θ)) = θ; outside it, the answer is the branch-representative (sin⁻¹(sin 2π/3) = π/3).…

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: "sin^-1 x + cos^-1 x = pi/2 for all x in [-1, 1]: the two inverses measure complementary arcs of the same triangle."

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: ***The triangle shortcut*** — for any inverse expression, draw the right triangle with the given ratio, read the third side from Pythagoras, and every addition formula becomes visible geometry.

rows.label: Limitation
rows.text: The branch is a choice that buys uniqueness: restrict the periodic function until it is one-to-one, and only then does the inverse exist.  ·  Principal branches: sin^-1 on [-1,1] -> [-pi/2, pi/2]; cos^-1 on [-1,1] -> [0, pi]; tan^-1 on R -> (-pi/2, pi/2); cot^-1 -> (0, pi); sec^-1, cosec^-1 on R minus (-1,1). Compositions: sin(sin^-1 x) = x on [-1,1]; sin^-1(sin th) = th only inside the branch (sin^-1(sin 2pi/3) = pi/3). Complement theorems: sin^-1 x + cos^-1 x = pi/2; tan^-1 x + cot^-1 x = pi/2; sec^-1 x + cosec^-1 x = pi/2.…

rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: ## 1. Topic Introduction — Undoing Periodic Functions sin, cos, tan are many-to-one; their **inverse circular functions** pick the **principal branch** — a restricted domain where each function is one-to-one — so the inverse is a genuine function. The theorems: principal value branches, inverse compositions, and the addition formulas for sin⁻¹ ± cos⁻¹/tan⁻¹.  ·  ## 2. Fundamental Concepts ### 2.1 Principal value branches (the core theorem) - **sin⁻¹:** domain [−1, 1], range **[−π/2, π/2]**. - **cos⁻¹:** domain [−1, 1], range **[0, π]**. - **tan⁻¹:** domain ℝ, range **(−π/2, π/2)**. - Proof idea: on these intervals each function is **bijective** (strictly monotone), so the inverse exists; the branch is *chosen* to make it so.…

rows.label: Shortcut
rows.text: Negative inputs: sine/tangent inverses are odd (keep the minus), cosine inverse gives pi - value. tan^-1 sums: check xy < 1 before the formula; correct by +- pi otherwise. sin^-1(sin th): reduce th into [-pi/2, pi/2] first.

rows.label: Board question
rows.text: **NEB 2024 (verified PYQ): Find the principal value of sin⁻¹(−1/2). (2m)** — Let **θ = sin⁻¹(−1/2)**. By definition sin θ = −1/2 **and θ must lie in the principal branch [−π/2, π/2]**. The reference angle whose sine is 1/2 is π/6; the negative sign places θ in the fourth quadrant of the branch, so **θ = −π/6**.…  ·  **NEB 2023 (verified PYQ): Find cos⁻¹(√3/2) + sin⁻¹(1/2). (2m)** — **First term:** cos⁻¹(√3/2) asks for the angle in the **cosine branch [0, π]** with cosine √3/2 — that is **π/6**. **Second term:** sin⁻¹(1/2) asks for the angle in the **sine branch [−π/2, π/2]** with sine 1/2 — that is **π/6**.…

rows.label: Hints
rows.text: Always state the branch when quoting a principal value — "pi/6, since it lies in [0, pi]" is a mark-bearing sentence.

rows.label: Universal facts
rows.text: Calculators return principal values only — that is why sin(150 degrees) needs you, not the machine, to say 30 degrees when the branch demands it.

rows.label: More practice
rows.text: **NEB-style (3m): Prove that tan⁻¹(1/2) + tan⁻¹(1/3) = π/4.** — **Check the condition:** xy = (1/2)(1/3) = 1/6 < 1, so the addition theorem applies without quadrant correction: tan⁻¹x + tan⁻¹y = tan⁻¹((x+y)/(1−xy)).…

rows.label: Study notes
rows.text: ## 3. Scientific Definitions | Term | Scientific meaning | Example | |---|---|---| | **Principal value** | The unique value of the inverse in the standard branch | sin⁻¹(1/2) = π/6, not 5π/6 | | **Principal branch** | Domain interval where the trig function is one-to-one | [−π/2, π/2] for sine | | **Inverse composition** | f(f⁻¹(x)) = x only inside the branch | sin⁻¹(sin 2π/3)…  ·  ## 4. Detailed Explanation ### 4.1 Why branches are necessary - sin θ = 1/2 holds for π/6, 5π/6, 13π/6, … — a function must return **one** value, so the inverse is defined only on a branch where the original is injective. The branch is a convention, but a universal one.…  ·  ## 5. Comparison Tables **Principal branches** | Function | Domain | Range (branch) | |---|---|---| | sin⁻¹ | [−1, 1] | [−π/2, π/2] | | cos⁻¹ | [−1, 1] | [0, π] | | tan⁻¹ | ℝ | (−π/2, π/2) | | cot⁻¹ | ℝ | (0, π) | | sec⁻¹ | ℝ∖(−1,1) | [0, π] − {π/2} | | cosec⁻¹ | ℝ∖(−1,1) | [−π/2, π/2] − {0} |

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: ## 6. Common Confusions **sin⁻¹(sin θ) ≠ θ in general:** only inside the branch; sin⁻¹(sin 120°) = 60°, not 120°.  ·  **sin⁻¹x is not 1/sin x:** the −1 is inverse-function notation, never a reciprocal — cosecant is the reciprocal.  ·  **cos⁻¹(−x) = π − cos⁻¹x:** negative inputs in cosine's branch reflect about π/2; the value stays in [0, π].

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: ## 7. Exam Application **NEB 2024 (verified PYQ): Find the principal value of sin⁻¹(−1/2). (2m)** — Let θ = sin⁻¹(−1/2), so sin θ = −1/2 with **θ ∈ [−π/2, π/2]** (the principal branch). The reference angle with sine 1/2 is π/6; the negative sign puts θ in the **fourth quadrant** of the branch: **θ = −π/6**.…  ·  **NEB 2023 (verified PYQ): Find cos⁻¹(√3/2) + sin⁻¹(1/2). (2m)** — **cos⁻¹(√3/2)**: cosine's branch is [0, π]; the angle with cosine √3/2 there is **π/6**. **sin⁻¹(1/2)**: sine's branch is [−π/2, π/2]; the angle is **π/6**. Sum: **π/6 + π/6 = π/3**.…  ·  **NEB-style (3m): Prove that tan⁻¹(1/2) + tan⁻¹(1/3) = π/4.** — Since xy = (1/2)(1/3) = 1/6 < 1, the addition theorem applies directly: tan⁻¹(1/2) + tan⁻¹(1/3) = tan⁻¹((1/2 + 1/3)/(1 − 1/6)) = tan⁻¹((5/6)/(5/6)) = **tan⁻¹(1) = π/4** (principal value in (−π/2, π/2)).…
